questiontext.text: Which classic algorithm compares the pattern against the text right-to-left, enabling large skips?

feedback.text: Correct — its bad-character and good-suffix rules exploit right-to-left scanning.
No — KMP scans left-to-right using its failure function.
No — Rabin-Karp compares hashes of left-to-right windows.
No — naive matching scans left-to-right with no skips.

generalfeedback.text: Boyer-Moore matches from the pattern's end, letting mismatches shift the pattern far ahead.

questiontext.text: Which algorithm identifies candidate matches using a rolling hash?

feedback.text: Correct — it slides a rolling hash over the text and compares hash values.
No — KMP uses a prefix/failure function, not hashing.
No — Boyer-Moore uses skip tables, not hashing.
No — the Z-algorithm uses the Z-array, not hashing.

generalfeedback.text: Rabin-Karp hashes each text window in O(1) amortized via a rolling hash, then verifies hits.

questiontext.text: Which algorithm precomputes a prefix/failure function (LPS) and never backtracks in the text?

feedback.text: Correct — the LPS table lets KMP advance the text pointer monotonically.
No — Boyer-Moore uses bad-character and good-suffix rules.
No — Rabin-Karp relies on hashing, not an LPS table.
No — naive matching does backtrack the text pointer.

generalfeedback.text: KMP's longest-proper-prefix-suffix (LPS) array tells it how far to shift the pattern without re-reading text.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Boyer-Moore are true? (select all that apply)

feedback.text: Yes — matching starts from the pattern's last character.

answer.text: It achieves sublinear average time with big skips on large alphabets

feedback.text: Yes — the bad-character rule shines when the alphabet is large.

answer.text: It uses a rolling hash to find candidates

feedback.text: No — that is Rabin-Karp.

answer.text: It is the best choice for searching many patterns at once

feedback.text: No — Rabin-Karp (or Aho-Corasick) handles multiple patterns better.

generalfeedback.text: Boyer-Moore is a single-pattern method: right-to-left scan, skip heuristics, sublinear on average for large alphabets.

questiontext.text: Among these three, which is best suited to searching for multiple patterns at once by hashing each pattern?

feedback.text: Correct — one text hash can be compared against a set of pattern hashes.
No — its skip tables are geared to a single pattern.
No — KMP's failure function is built for one pattern.

generalfeedback.text: By storing many pattern hashes in a set, Rabin-Karp screens for any of them in one pass.

questiontext.text: KMP, Boyer-Moore, and Rabin-Karp all solve the exact string matching problem.

feedback.text: Correct — all three report exact occurrences; they differ in strategy.
All three do find exact matches.

questiontext.text: KMP runs in O(n + m) worst-case time, and Rabin-Karp runs in O(n + m) on average.

feedback.text: Correct — KMP is linear worst-case; Rabin-Karp is linear on average (worst case O(n*m)).
KMP is O(n+m) worst-case and Rabin-Karp is O(n+m) average.
